summary: DNSSEC relies on cryptographic algorithms that must interoperate. This document sets out the process for updating recommendations on which algorithms implementations should support. It obsoletes RFC 8624 and updates RFC 9157.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC signs DNS data with a choice of cryptographic algorithms, and every implementation has to agree on at least one of them. This document moves the list of recommended algorithms out of an RFC and into the two IANA registries, so that a future RFC can change one algorithm's status without rewriting the whole list.

questions: where is the dnssec algorithm list kept
subtitle: How the list of DNSSEC algorithms that software must support is kept, and how it changes over time.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC only works if resolvers and authoritative servers share at least one signing algorithm, so the set of algorithms everyone must support has to be written down somewhere and kept current.
tldr.mechanism: The canonical list moves out of an RFC and into the two IANA DNSSEC algorithm registries, which gain four columns each: two for what to deploy and two for what to implement. Future documents change the values in those columns.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9904 obsoletes RFC 8624 and updates RFC 9157. It does not change the status of any algorithm listed in RFC 8624, and it moves the registry entries for private use and the reserved ranges.

facts.label: Digest values reserved for private use

today: RFC 9904 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8624 and updates RFC 9157, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It changes no algorithm's recommendation status; the initial values are the ones from RFC 8624.

sections.title: Moving the Algorithm List to the Registries
sections.content:
DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) is used to provide authentication of DNS data, and the DNSSEC signing algorithms are defined by various RFCs. To ensure interoperability, a set of mandatory-to-implement DNS Public Key (DNSKEY) algorithms is defined. This document moves the canonical status of the algorithms from RFC 8624 to the IANA DNSSEC algorithm registries, so that the current status is more easily accessible and future changes are easier to publish. It also incorporates the revised IANA DNSSEC considerations from RFC 9157, and adds recommendations about which algorithms should be deployed regardless of implementation status.

This mirrors the process used for the TLS Cipher Suites registry, where the canonical list of cipher suites lives in the IANA registry and RFCs reference the registry. Extensions to the DNSSEC registries can be made in future RFCs.

This document does not change the recommendation status of the algorithms listed in RFC 8624; that is the work of future documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of algorithms that DNSSEC software has to support used to live in a document that had to be replaced every time one entry changed. The list now lives in the IANA registries, and a future RFC only needs to change a single row.

sections.title: Downgrading an Algorithm Over Time
sections.content:
By the time a DNSSEC cryptographic algorithm is made mandatory to implement, it should already be available in most implementations. The recommendation status of each algorithm is expected to change over time: there is no guarantee that a newly introduced algorithm will become mandatory to implement, and published algorithms are continuously subjected to cryptographic attack and may become too weak, or even completely broken.

Deprecation of an algorithm is expected to be gradual, so that implementations have time to update while remaining interoperable. Unless there are strong security reasons, an algorithm is expected to be downgraded from MUST to NOT RECOMMENDED or MAY, instead of directly from MUST to MUST NOT. An algorithm that has not been mentioned as mandatory to implement is expected to be introduced as RECOMMENDED instead of a MUST.

Because using an unknown DNSKEY algorithm makes the zone be treated as insecure, algorithms that have been downgraded to NOT RECOMMENDED or lower should not be used by authoritative nameservers and DNSSEC signers to create new DNSKEYs, so that the use of deprecated algorithms decreases over time. Once an algorithm has reached a sufficiently low level of deployment it can be marked MUST NOT, so that recursive resolvers can remove support for validating it. Validating recursive resolvers are encouraged to retain support for all algorithms not marked as MUST NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: An algorithm that turns out to be weak is not banned overnight. It is first downgraded to not recommended, so that operators stop signing with it while validators keep accepting it, and only much later, once hardly anyone uses it, is it marked as must not be used at all.

sections.title: The Four New Columns in Each Registry
sections.content:
Four columns have been added to the DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry: Use for DNSSEC Signing, Use for DNSSEC Validation, Implement for DNSSEC Signing, and Implement for DNSSEC Validation. The Use for DNSSEC Signing column indicates the recommendation for using the algorithm within authoritative servers, Use for DNSSEC Validation the recommendation for using it in DNSSEC validators, Implement for DNSSEC Signing the recommendation for implementing it within DNSSEC signing software, and Implement for DNSSEC Validation the recommendation for implementing it within DNSSEC validators.

The Digest Algorithms registry gains the same four columns with different wording: Use for DNSSEC Delegation, Use for DNSSEC Validation, Implement for DNSSEC Delegation, and Implement for DNSSEC Validation.

Only the values MAY, RECOMMENDED, MUST NOT and NOT RECOMMENDED may be placed in the two Use for columns, while the two Implement for columns may also hold MUST. A value of MUST is not an allowed value for the two Use for columns.
sections.plainLanguage: Each registry now says two things about every algorithm: whether you should deploy it, and whether your software should support it. Deploying and supporting are judged separately, because software usually gains support for an algorithm before operators start using it.

sections.title: Adding and Changing Registry Values
sections.content:
A note has been added to both registries describing how values are added and changed. Adding a new entry with a recommended value of MAY in any of the four columns follows the Specification Required policy of RFC 8126, which promotes continued evolution of DNSSEC algorithms and DNSSEC agility. New entries added through the Specification Required process have the value MAY for all columns. Adding a new entry, or changing an existing value, to anything other than MAY in any of the four columns requires Standards Action.

The same note points out that an item which is not marked as RECOMMENDED does not necessarily mean that it is flawed. Rather, it indicates that the item either has not been through the IETF consensus process, has limited applicability, or is intended only for specific use cases.

The initial values were transcribed from RFC 8624 for the Implement for columns. The Use for columns were set to the same values, because the general interpretation to date indicates they have been treated as values for both use and implementation, with the value in the Use for column shown as RECOMMENDED when the corresponding Implement for value is MUST. The two kinds of value may diverge in the future, as implementations generally precede deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: New algorithms arrive with the weakest possible status, which a lighter review process can set, and only a full standards review can raise or lower them. A value that is not recommended is not a verdict on the algorithm itself; it may simply mean the algorithm has not been through the full review, or is meant for a narrow purpose.

sections.title: The Initial Values for DNSSEC Algorithms
sections.content:
Table 2 of the document sets out the initial values for the DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry. RSAMD5, DSA, DSA-NSEC3-SHA1 and ECC-GOST are MUST NOT in all four columns. RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 are NOT RECOMMENDED for signing and RECOMMENDED for validation, and NOT RECOMMENDED to implement for signing but MUST to implement for validation. RSASHA256 and ECDSAP256SHA256 are RECOMMENDED for both uses and MUST to implement for both. RSASHA512 is NOT RECOMMENDED for signing and RECOMMENDED for validation. ECC-GOST is MAY for both uses. ECDSAP384SHA384 and ED448 are MAY for signing, RECOMMENDED for validation, MAY to implement for signing and RECOMMENDED to implement for validation. ED25519 is RECOMMENDED for both uses and RECOMMENDED to implement for both. SM2SM3, ECC-GOST12, PRIVATEDNS and PRIVATEOID are MAY in all four columns.

Table 3 gives the initial values for the Digest Algorithms registry, which covers the digest used in Delegation Signer (DS) resource records. The value 0, NULL (CDS only), is MUST NOT everywhere. SHA-1 is MUST NOT for delegation and for implementing delegation, but RECOMMENDED for validation and MUST to implement for validation. SHA-256 is RECOMMENDED for both delegation and validation and MUST to implement for both. GOST R 34.11-94 is MUST NOT for delegation and MAY for validation. SHA-384 is MAY for delegation, RECOMMENDED for validation, MAY to implement for delegation and RECOMMENDED to implement for validation. GOST R 34.11-2012 and SM3 are MAY in all four columns.

When there are multiple RECOMMENDED algorithms in the Use for columns, operators should choose the best algorithm according to local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables say which algorithms are recommended today. For signing DNS data, RSASHA256, ECDSAP256SHA256 and ED25519 are recommended; RSASHA1 and RSASHA512 are not recommended for signing though still acceptable for checking; MD5 and DSA must not be used. For the digests in delegation records, SHA-256 is recommended and SHA-1 is still acceptable for checking but must not be used for delegation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of cryptographic systems depends on the strength of both the cryptographic algorithms chosen and the keys used with those algorithms, and on the engineering of the protocol used by the system so that there are no non-cryptographic ways to bypass the security of the overall system.

This document concerns itself with the selection of cryptographic algorithms for DNSSEC, specifically with the selection of mandatory-to-implement algorithms. The algorithms identified as MUST or RECOMMENDED to implement are not known to be broken at the current time, and cryptographic research so far leads the authors to believe that they are likely to remain adequately secure unless a significant and unexpected discovery is made. That is not necessarily forever, and future documents are expected from time to time to reflect the current best practice.

Retiring an algorithm too soon would result in a zone signed with the retired algorithm being downgraded to the equivalent of an unsigned zone. Algorithm deprecation must therefore be done only after careful consideration, and ideally slowly when possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithms listed as required or recommended are not known to be broken. Pulling one out of service too quickly would make the zones that still use it look unsigned to validators, which is why the document insists on a slow, careful retirement.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
DNSKEY algorithm rollover in a live zone is a complex process, and the document points to the guidelines in RFC 6781 and RFC 7583 for how to perform algorithm rollovers.

DS algorithm rollover in a live zone is also a complex process. Upgrading an algorithm at the same time as rolling to the new Key Signing Key (KSK) key leads to DNSSEC validation failures, and users must upgrade the DS algorithm first before rolling to a new KSK.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the algorithm of a live zone is delicate. The digest that parents use to point at a zone has to be changed before the zone's own key is replaced, otherwise validators see a mismatch and the zone looks broken.

sections.title: What IANA Changed
sections.content:
IANA has updated the DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry with the four new columns, populated with the values from Table 2 of the document, and has completed three further actions: it changed the registration procedure to Standards Action or Specification Required, added a note describing the values that are not marked as RECOMMENDED, and listed this document as an additional reference for the registry.

IANA has made the same set of changes to the Digest Algorithms registry, with the values from Table 3: the four new columns, the registration procedure change, the note about values not marked as RECOMMENDED, and this document as an additional reference. It has also marked the values 128-252 as Reserved, marked the values 253 and 254 as Reserved for Private Use, and deleted the now superfluous column named Status from the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The registries themselves have been reorganised: new columns, a simpler registration procedure, a note explaining what an unrecommended value means, and the private-use range set aside for algorithms that are not on the list.
